public_rationale: Marcus wrote on 2026-06-10 that core reliability and factuality problems had not been solved. On 2026-04-23, Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmark operator, reported hallucination rates on its AA-Omniscience knowledge benchmark. When the models did not answer correctly, they often gave a wrong answer instead of declining. The rate was 86% for GPT-5.5, 50% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and 36% for Claude Opus 4.7 (e1). The same source said GPT-5.5's gain over GPT-5.4 came mostly from knowledge, with a modest improvement in hallucination (e1). A secondary summary reports that OpenAI's system card found GPT-5.5's claims 23% more likely to be correct than GPT-5.4's, with factual errors 3% less often (e2). These gains are measured against the previous model and do not show that errors were eliminated. Neither source shows near-zero error rates in the period. Under the plain reading, the claim holds.
limitations: AA-Omniscience uses hard knowledge questions and measures how often a model answers wrongly instead of declining. It does not show error rates on everyday tasks.
'Reliability' is broader than factuality. This assessment uses hallucination measures only.
The system-card figures come from a secondary summary, not the card itself.
There is no agreed threshold for when hallucination counts as solved.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: in the months before the post, leading frontier LLMs still made factual errors (hallucinations) at material rates on independent tests. That means the problem was not fixed, even if it was improving.
'Solved' is read as: hallucination brought down to a level where outputs can be trusted without checking. Partial gains do not count as solved.
criteria.support_condition: Independent or company tests published in roughly March to June 2026 show current frontier models still give confident wrong answers or factual errors at substantial rates.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evaluations from that period show frontier models with near-zero hallucination or factual error rates on standard factuality benchmarks, so that reliability could fairly be called solved.
